Found while building the folio's pair (066), where the headline was made a rollup of the per-folio rows for exactly this reason: a headline that is a sum of its breakdown cannot contradict it. 066 also shows what makes two implementations honest when one is kept for a measured reason — one is named the authority, and an assertion compares the pair on EVERY row rather than a sample. The stock pair has neither
An assertion that the rebuilt totals equal the old ones on the live rows, so the rebuild is proven to change no figure

A SCHEDULED DEEP CHECK FOR EVERY PAIR THIS PRODUCT KEEPS ON PURPOSE, folio and stock, on the monthly restore-test slot: compare both implementations across a property and report the rows that disagree. This is the half 066 could not do inline — folio_gl_reconciliation does not compare folio_totals with folio_totals_by_folio, or folio_posting_state with folio_posting_states, because comparing per document is the 20-second path the set-wise forms exist to avoid. So the apply-day assertions are the floor and this is the ceiling, and without it 'the pair is pinned' means 'was pinned once'
shipments.proof: Run both before and after: every column of the property totals identical, on live data. Then change the per-position query and watch the totals follow.
shipments.note: NAMED RATHER THAN LEFT AS SOMETHING EVERYBODY KNOWS. It is not urgent — no figure is wrong today — but it is a correctness risk on a module that is live and read, and the folio side now carries the better pattern, so the two halves of the product would otherwise drift apart in how they are built as well as in what they say. AND IT CARRIES THE ANSWER FOR BOTH PAIRS, because 066 left the folio side with the same hole in a milder form: where two implementations of one rule are kept for a MEASURED reason, the pin cannot be inline — comparing per document is precisely the cost the set-wise form exists to remove — so it is SCHEDULED. A deep check function per pair, comparing both implementations across a property and reporting any disagreement with the rows that differ, run on the SAME MONTHLY SLOT AS THE RESTORE TEST. Expensive proof on a schedule rather than inline is a pattern this repo already has and already trusts, and it is the only honest form of 'the pair is pinned' once the inline version has been measured and rejected. One shipment, two pairs: rebuild the stock headline as a rollup of its breakdown, and give both pairs their scheduled check.

ships: LANDED: THE REFUND BUTTON, which closes a gap this project opened itself. 067 shut the door where a refund was a minus sign in the payment box with no approval, no reason and no limit — and left the act unreachable, because record_refund had no caller. A FOLIO-LEVEL button beside Take payment, never a row action on a payment: record_refund takes a folio and has no payment as its target, which is the same property that made record_refund the right name, and the act that DOES target a payment is already on that payment's menu as Reverse

LANDED: THE EFFECT LINE STATES THE RESULTING BALANCE, NOT A DIRECTION, and the first draft was wrong in the way that reads fluently. 'The balance goes up by X — the guest owes that again' is true above zero and FALSE below it: 50,000 received against no charges, refund 20,000, balance -50,000 to -30,000, and the guest owed nothing before OR after. It now names the resulting Outstanding Balance in the bill's own label and sign, and characterises it only when the figure does — BalanceRow's rule verbatim. The proof drives all three sides of zero plus the crossing case, because a fixture on the owing side alone would have passed the drafted sentence

LANDED: the ceiling SHOWN and never prefilled, and the distinction said out loud rather than left to be re-litigated — a figure displayed tells somebody the limit before they type, a figure in the box gets accepted without being read (rule 10). The button is disabled exactly where record_refund refuses and nowhere else, measured against the live function on all three statuses: OPEN and SETTLED allowed, CLOSED refused with 23514. No explanatory line under it, as Add charge carries none

LANDED: and a finding from that measurement — on a CLOSED folio the PIN is spent BEFORE the refusal lands, because record_refund verifies the manager and then delegates to record_payment, which owns the folio-status rule. Harmless now the button is disabled there, and the reason the button had to be rather than merely ought to be

LANDED: the FIRST FOLIO SURFACE to use the shared ManagerPinField. Four reversal forms plus DiscountForm still hand-roll a block identical to it; that conversion is 1.1h4b1 and deliberately not folded in, because a refund proof that also rewrote three money screens could no longer tell the refund form is right from I touched three other screens. ManagerPinField's own header claimed its defaults were the reversal wording the four folio forms use when none of them import it — rule 28 in a comment, corrected here with a self-expiring adoption list

LANDED: 32 render-proof assertions, 10 breakages, all 10 caught — and ONE of them caught the PROOF. The prefill check looked for a name attribute this codebase never renders, so it matched nothing, undefined satisfied it, and prefilling the field with the ceiling produced NO RED. The assertion meant to catch this proof's headline defect was decoration (rule 27), and the breakage run is the only reason that is known

LANDED: THE SAME STALE INSTRUCTION LIVED IN FOUR PLACES and 067 fixed one. A refund is a negative amount was in the field's help text (067), in PAYMENT_ABOUT's panel above it, and TWICE in the staff guide — including There is no separate refund button. One behaviour change, four copies of the instruction, each found only by looking. All four now corrected

AND THE GAP IT CLOSED, kept on the record rather than erased: between 067 and this shipment a partial refund was reachable only through SQL. 067 shut the door where a refund was a minus sign with no approval and no reason, and in doing so removed the only UI route to giving PART of a payment back. Reversing a WHOLE payment still worked from the screen with its own PIN, so a full give-back was reachable — a guest who paid 50,000 and left early owed 20,000 back was not. Stating it was the point; an unstated gap is the thing we do not do
Its own render proof, because the split between this and item 10 is the SCREEN: item 10 is the Accounts screen and its proof, this is the payment screen and its proof
shipments.proof: Take a payment, refund part of it with a reason and a manager PIN, and watch the folio balance and the guest ledger agree. Then try to refund more than came in and read the refusal.
shipments.note: PARTIAL REFUNDS ARE REACHABLE AGAIN, which they were not between 067 and this. SPLIT OUT OF 1.1h4 ITEM 10 DELIBERATELY. Item 10 already carried five pieces plus a migration, and two screens is two render proofs. It is next with nothing between, because the gap it closes was opened by 067 rather than inherited. FILED UNDER 1.1h4 AND NOT 1.1h5: a guest refund is not a supplier payment, and the gap exists because of 1.1h4, so the next reader finds the fix under the shipment that created the need for it without reconstructing why. It also sorts ahead of 1.1h4b, which is where 'next with nothing between' belongs.

ships: ReverseChargeForm, ReversePaymentForm, ReverseBookingStatusForm, ReverseCheckoutForm and DiscountForm adopt the shared ManagerPinField, which seven surfaces already use — six on the stock and purchasing side and, from 1.1h4a, the refund form

IT IS DUPLICATION RATHER THAN TWO SOURCES OF TRUTH, which is why it has waited: all five render the same type, inputMode, autoComplete and maxLength, and the database is the actual guard either way. Nothing is wrong today. What is wrong is that the next surface needing a PIN has two patterns to copy from

DiscountForm is the one that is not a straight swap: its panel is threshold-gated rather than always shown, which is why ManagerPinField takes its lead sentence as a prop at all. It converts last and proves that branch

Its own render proof, and the claim is a different one from any shipment that built a form: that all five render AS THEY DID BEFORE. A visual-regression assertion, which is why folding it into 1.1h4a would have muddied that proof's claim — the refund form is right and I touched three other money screens are not the same green
And ManagerPinField's adoption list gets DELETED when this lands, as its header says: a list of who has adopted a component is worth keeping only while the answer is not everybody
shipments.proof: Each of the five screens before and after: the same markup, the same PIN behaviour, the same refusal from the database. Then break the shared component once and watch all five proofs go red together, which is the point of there being one.
shipments.note: RAISED WHILE BUILDING 1.1h4a, which became ManagerPinField's first folio consumer and so the first place the duplication was visible from inside the folio module. The component was extracted during a stock shipment with the folio forms' own wording copied into its defaults, and its header claimed those forms used it — corrected in 1.1h4a. Five hand-rolled copies is not a bug; it is the thing that becomes one the day somebody changes the PIN wording in four places and misses the fifth.

shipments.t: A credential is the last thing asked for
ships: LANDED (069): THREE FUNCTIONS REORDERED so every precondition that cannot be satisfied by fetching a manager is tested BEFORE the PIN is demanded. A PIN is the most expensive check in the product because it is the only one that moves a human across a room. No new rule, no new permission, no signature change: the same acts succeed and the same acts fail, and what changes is whether somebody walks first

LANDED (069): the census that scoped it — FOURTEEN functions call verify_manager_pin, found by syntax then each read in place, and TWELVE WERE ALREADY CORRECT. That is a house pattern nobody had written down, which is how the other two happened; it is now rule 9a in CLAUDE.md with the THREE legitimate exceptions named, because without them the next reader reorders apply_charge_discount and breaks it: the PIN decision itself, a replay check inside a unique_violation handler, and a courtesy refusal of a PIN that was not needed

LANDED (069): reverse_purchase_receipt is the instance that justifies the file — the only one reachable today. It demanded the PIN and THEN checked whether the delivery had already been reversed, which is the likeliest state in the building to change between a page load and a submit: two people clearing the same mistake. The storekeeper opened the screen, a colleague reversed it first, the storekeeper walked to find a manager, the manager typed their PIN, and the system then said it was done on the 5th

LANDED (069): record_refund gained a closed-folio refusal AT THE REFUND DOOR, before the PIN, with a DISTINCT errcode (PT407). record_payment refuses it underneath and keeps refusing it — it owns the rule and is the floor. What it does not own is the sentence: its message is 'cannot take payments', which is right at its door and wrong at one where somebody is handing money BACK. A distinct code is what lets an assertion tell which layer spoke (rule 27's sixth shape)

LANDED (069): and TWO OF THE THREE ARE UNREACHABLE TODAY, reordered anyway, with the reason in the header so the next reader does not delete it as dead work. Nothing in this build writes folios.status. A guard written correctly before it matters costs one migration; the same guard remembered later costs a manager standing at a terminal for nothing

LANDED (069): receive_purchase_order LEFT ALONE, with a TRIGGER rather than a 'later' (044's model). Its one out-of-order check sits inside the per-line work loop, so hoisting it means a pre-pass over p_lines in a 535-line delivery function on a money path, to beat an admin retiring an expense category mid-receipt. THE DAY THAT FUNCTION NEEDS A PRE-PASS FOR ANY OTHER REASON, THIS CHECK JOINS IT. reverse_purchase_receipt's own per-line check stays for the same reason and to be consistent about it

LANDED (069): AND THE COMMENT THE DECISION RESTED ON WAS TESTED RATHER THAN BELIEVED, on 7 November. reverse_purchase_receipt's per-line check was left unhoisted because its own comment calls it belt-and-braces for old data and unreachable going forward — a sentence promising that a state cannot arise, which is rule 28's shape exactly. VERIFIED BY BEHAVIOUR, three ways, rolled back: a census established that only post_movement_reversal and its three callers can put a reversals row on a stock movement; reverse_stock_movement aimed at a delivery-sourced movement REFUSES BY NAME (PT409, 'this stock arrived on a delivery'); that movement's source_document_type is purchase_receipt, and ZERO delivery lines anywhere carry a stock-take movement; and ZERO existing delivery lines carry a movement reversal, so the belt-and-braces half has nothing to catch either. The comment is TRUE, and the decision not to hoist stands on a measurement instead of on a sentence

LANDED (069): 11 assertions, 8 breakages, all 8 red — and the shape that makes a reordering testable at all is a WRONG PIN with an already-impossible request: the refusal must name the act. With a valid PIN the precondition refuses either way and the order is invisible. TWO OF THE EIGHT MUTATIONS WERE NO-OPS BEFORE THEY WERE FIXED, both reporting the code as passing, which is rule 27's seventh shape applied to the harness rather than the proof
shipments.proof: Reverse a delivery, then try again with a WRONG manager PIN: the refusal names the delivery as already reversed rather than asking for a PIN. Then put the old order back and watch it go red.
shipments.note: SCOPED FROM A CENSUS RATHER THAN FROM ONE FUNCTION, because one function is not a pattern. The ruling that opened it asserted that night audit closes folios between a page load and a submit; nothing in this build closes a folio, and checking that rather than inheriting it is what turned up the larger finding on 1.1a1. The PRINCIPLE needed no reachable instance; the instance that exists is better than the one that was assumed.

shipments.t: The sweep: posting what has come due
ships: A folio document whose business date is still ahead posts NOTHING when it is written (062): revenue for the 7th belongs to the 7th, and post_journal refuses a future-dated entry because rules 8 and 12 already said so. Something has to post it when the day arrives, and that is this

It lives in the NIGHT AUDIT, which already runs once a day at the property's cutoff and is already idempotent through the document pair (tenant, source type, source id). A sweep buried inside a wiring migration is a thing nobody can find when it misfires
It posts every folio_charge, folio_charge_discount and folio_payment whose business date has come and which has no entry — bounded and paged, never an unbounded scan (rule 1a)
It reports what it posted and what it could not, in the audit's own summary jsonb, so a morning with a refusal is visible rather than silent
RE-RUNNABLE BY CONSTRUCTION: a second run the same morning posts nothing, because post_journal hands back the existing entry on the document pair. Asserted rather than assumed
shipments.proof: Check a four-night guest out on arrival day: one entry tonight, three nights waiting. Move the clock forward a day and run the audit: the second night posts, dated to itself, at its own locked rate. Run it twice and nothing changes.
shipments.note: Its own item because 062 established the need and must not also answer it. The decline in post_folio_charge_journal is what creates the backlog; this is what drains it, and item 8's not_yet_due bucket is what makes the backlog readable in between. Small, but it is the difference between a ledger that is behind by a known amount and one that is behind.

shipments.t: A mapping cannot be pulled from under a category
ships: A trigger refusing to DELETE or deactivate an account_mappings row that a live charge category or tax charge still points at, with the hint NAMING what depends on it

The other half of a rule that is currently guarded in one direction only. enforce_charge_category_account (044) already refuses to point a category at an unmapped role key, on INSERT and on UPDATE — and then an admin can delete the mapping underneath it, or deactivate the account it points at, and the next charge in that category fails at the counter with a guest standing there
ONE DIRECTION GUARDED AND THE OTHER OPEN READS AS 'GUARDED' TO THE NEXT PERSON, which is worse than neither: the reviewer who sees the category trigger stops looking

Refuse at the moment of the DECISION, not at the moment of the consequence — 052's expense-category ruling in a third place. The person who unmaps an account is not the person who meets the refusal, and they are days apart
044's loud failure at the posting site stays as the floor. This is the interface
shipments.proof: Map a category, then try to delete its mapping: refused, naming the category. Deactivate the account instead: refused the same way. Delete a mapping nothing points at: allowed.
shipments.note: Named rather than squeezed into 062, where it would have been a trigger nobody asked for in a migration about wiring. account_mappings has an admin DELETE policy and an admin UPDATE policy, so this is reachable from the Accounts screen today, not theoretical.

shipments.t: A forward date gets its own errcode
ships: A DISTINCT errcode for 'this document cannot be dated in the future', carried by post_charge (062) and record_payment (063), separate from post_journal's PT422 for 'this JOURNAL ENTRY cannot be dated in the future'

Rule 27's sixth shape is what asks for it: an assertion read the sqlstate AND the message and was still satisfied by the WRONG refusal, because two layers refuse the same act with the same code and overlapping prose. A pattern on prose is the floor; the code is the interface — the same sentence as the unique index and the lookup

THE TWO REFUSALS MEAN OPPOSITE THINGS to the person at the screen. post_charge or record_payment refusing is a date rejected at the keystroke. post_journal refusing means the row was already written and the transaction died on the way to the ledger — a cashier told the ledger rejected their takings. A client that switches on the code can tell them apart; one that matches prose cannot
Both assertions re-pointed at the new code, and a breakage confirming that post_journal's refusal no longer satisfies either
shipments.proof: Delete post_charge's forward-date refusal and the assertion goes red naming the code, not merely the sentence. Key a forward-dated payment and read the errcode the client receives.
shipments.note: Its own file rather than smuggled into 063, which is about wiring discounts and payments: 062 is already applied history, so a consistent answer re-emits two functions for a reason unrelated to either shipment. 063 meets the FLOOR — its assertion matches on 'A payment cannot be dated...', naming its subject — so nothing is unproven today; this raises it to the interface.

ships: A payment document: who was paid, from which account, on what date, by what method
Allocation against receipts, explicit and reversible, reversed by counter-entry like everything else
An advance is a payment with nothing allocated yet, and it posts a journal like any other. No special case with no entry, which is the bug the ERP needed two migrations to unwind
Supplier activity becomes a supplier account, with a balance that is the sum of the documents and no stored mirror column
A statement that paginates and excludes voided entries, neither of which the ERP's does
Withholding tax deducted at payment where the supplier carries a rate
shipments.proof: Receive ₦500,000 of goods across two orders, pay ₦300,000 against one of them. The supplier balance reads ₦200,000, the payable account in the books agrees with it to the kobo, and the statement shows both documents in order.
shipments.note: Pulled forward out of stage 7 by a question from Lanre about supplier management. Receiving credits supplier payable and nothing in the plan ever debited it, so Heledon's first trial balance would have carried a liability that had never once gone down. An account that only grows is not a book. What stays in stage 7 is the depth: approvals and spend limits, price history and comparison, ageing analytics.

ships: A payment FROM a company: who paid, into which account, on what date, by what method — the mirror of 1.1h5's supplier payment and deliberately nothing more
Allocation against what that company owes, explicit and reversible, reversed by counter-entry like everything else
It DEBITS nothing and CREDITS company_receivable, which is the whole point: today the account can only grow
A company account that is the SUM OF ITS DOCUMENTS with no stored balance column (rule 6), paginated and excluding voided rows (rules 1b, 5)
NOT invoicing, NOT ageing, NOT one invoice covering many stays. Those stay at 9.3 where they are
shipments.proof: Settle a corporate stay to the company account, then record the company paying part of it. The company balance falls by what was paid, company_receivable in the books agrees with it, and reversing the payment puts both back.
shipments.note: PULLED FORWARD INTO GO-LIVE, for the reason 1.1h5 was. 062 wired company_account — a payment by that method debits company_receivable, because nothing was received: the debt moves from the guest to the company. Nothing anywhere in the codebase credits it, and the path that would (9.3) sits two milestones out, so the balance sheet has a second account that can only go one way. 046's header had already written the same sentence about supplier_payable: 'Receiving CREDITS supplier_payable, and NOTHING IN THIS SHIPMENT EVER DEBITS' — which is why 1.1h5 moved. REACHABLE, not theoretical: the account is mapped (1210), company_account is live on the payment picker, bookings have carried company_id since 015, one company already has negotiated rates, and mark_no_show charges only a GUARANTEED booking, which means a company one. The first corporate booking Heledon takes starts the balance. THE REALISTIC FIRST TEST OF THIS SHIPMENT IS A GUARANTEED NO-SHOW: mark_no_show charges only a booking with a company or billed to one, so the first charge in the whole product that will settle against company_receivable is a guest who never arrived. Learned by asserting a charge on a guest-billed no-show and getting none — 062's fixture was wrong and the code was right.

shipments.t: Outlet prices and the bulk price tool

Bulk update: pick a location, optionally a category, raise by a percentage or set a value
Preview before commit showing before and after per item and a count of what changes
Delta writes only, never a full replace, every change logged
Rounding rule, default nearest ₦10, configurable
shipments.proof: Raise all Drinks prices in the Bar by 10%, see the preview, commit, and confirm the Restaurant prices did not move and a sale posted yesterday still shows yesterday's price.
shipments.note: Was 1.1h. Moved down one so purchasing lands first: a hotel buys before it sells, and an outlet price only moves a figure on a screen until something can be sold.

ships: One sheet creates the item and, for a brand-new item only, its opening balance
A row whose name already exists is skipped whole, definition and quantity both, so a double upload can never double stock
Every column: name, code, type, base unit, category, barcode, pack size, purchase cost, min, max, reorder level, selling price, opening quantity, unit cost, location
Location defaults to the store and can only hold a store
Corrected sample set: 14 rows covering all three types, seven units and all eight categories, every row valid against the seeded reference data
Instructions on their own green tab in the xlsx, out of the CSV entirely, and rendered in the app on the download panel
An unknown unit or category asks once and is created on confirmation, never silently
Similarity prompt on units and categories, the protection item names already have
shipments.proof: Download and re-upload untouched: every sample row skipped, nothing created. Fill it with a new unit, a new category and a near-duplicate category: three distinct questions, import blocked until answered. Re-upload the filled file: nothing created twice and no quantity moves.
shipments.note: Last of the inventory shipments because a template can only offer a column that already exists behind it. The sheet gets touched once, not twice. Once it lands, day one for a new hotel is a single file, which is also what shipment 13.2 needs. Was 1.1i.

shipments.t: Inventory end-to-end walkthrough, by a human
ships: Lanre clicks the whole inventory module through as a storekeeper and a manager would
Every screen 1.1c to 1.1h exercised against a ZZ Test sandbox location and item
Feedback fed back as fixes before stage 2 starts
shipments.proof: A full day's inventory work — create, load, receive, issue, adjust, count, reverse, write off, reprice — done end to end without asking anyone how, and the numbers reconcile.
shipments.note: Agreed 16 Aug: per-shipment click-throughs are deferred and batched here, since Code's SQL proofs already run on the live DB. The exception is 1.1c, which gets a short look on its own because every later screen copies its reversal dialog pattern. Was 1.1j. Now covers purchasing too.

ships: 3 Vercel env vars for the night-audit cron (CRON_SECRET, service key, URL)
Rotate the .env.local DB password to alphanumeric
Server statement locale printing NGN instead of ₦
Fix the useBookingDraft memoisation trap at source
shipments.proof: Cron fires unattended overnight and posts the right nights; emailed PDF shows ₦; no effect loop when a draft key is watched directly

shipments.t: Security sweep: revoke anon on every RPC
ships: Audit every SECURITY DEFINER function shipped so far
REVOKE ALL FROM public, anon then GRANT to authenticated
In-migration assertion that anon EXECUTE is false
Confirm no internal guard relies on auth.uid() IS NOT NULL

FLAGS REACHABLE THROUGH PostgREST THAT NO SCREEN OFFERS, decided as a set rather than one at a time. SEVEN today: p_allow_negative on the STOCK side (post_stock_adjustment, post_stock_writeoff) and now p_allow_negative on record_payment too (067, same name on purpose — it is the house pattern, and the list has to name both), p_allow_unvalued (the same two stock functions), p_allow_moved_stock (finish_stock_take), p_count_no_show (count_available), p_post_journal (post_stock_receipt AND record_payment, 065) and p_allow_future (post_charge, 062). SEVEN. PostgREST passes whatever named arguments a request carries, so any of them can be set by a staff user even where no UI offers it. The boundary has always been is_tenant_staff and RLS rather than the absence of a parameter, and these flags are a CONFIRMATION of an override — but some are offered in a dialog and some are not, and the ones that are not may belong behind a function nothing grants. This is the place to look at all six together: deciding them one at a time inside unrelated shipments is how you end up with five answers
shipments.proof: A query listing anon-executable functions returns only the intended public readers
shipments.note: This exact hole bit Palstro ERP twice. Sweep it before real staff and real guests are on the system.

shipments.t: Monitoring, nightly backup and a proven restore
ships: Twice-daily encrypted backup of the whole database, both Lagos slots, taken by a read-only login that can read every row but write nothing
The images backed up too, verified byte for byte and checksummed, because the bucket is the only copy of them
A manifest recorded at backup time: every table's row count, the counters as values, the GL wiring stamp. The restore test asserts against it rather than against a list somebody chose
A monthly restore into a throwaway database that proves the backup opens and everything the manifest claims about it is true
The backup refuses to run at all if a private bucket appears, rather than silently skipping it
Failure opens one issue, comments on repeats, and closes itself on the next good run
Secrets audited by a check-setup run that names anything missing instead of failing eight seconds in
shipments.proof: Run live on 2 November: 26 setup checks green, a 1.7 MB encrypted artifact in 65 seconds, then restored into a throwaway Postgres and verified, 8 passed, 0 failed, 2 correctly reported as vacuous. Every assertion was made to fail first, including lying to it about the stock movements.
shipments.note: Pulled forward from after go-live because the books now hold data that cannot be rebuilt from migrations: the chart of accounts, its mappings, the audit trail, and gl_wired_at, which cannot be re-derived from anything. Copied from the Palstro Fuel design rather than the ERP one, because fuel's is the ERP's with each of its failures already fixed. Three things improved on fuel in passing: the project ref derived from the connection string rather than hardcoded, so a backup pointed at the wrong project is caught structurally; storage taken with no new credential at all, since the backup login can already list the objects and the bucket is public; and checks that cannot tell working from absent report themselves as vacuous rather than passing. Found on the way, and worth more than the backup: the keep-alive workflow had failed all 34 times it ran since 1 October, because two secrets were never added. It looked like a safety net in the sidebar. The project stayed awake on the owner's own dashboard activity. Standing rule added: a scheduled job that has never succeeded looks identical to one that has never been needed, so every scheduled job gets a run read by a human within a week of being added. Owed: a first storage recovery drill. The upload half of the runbook has never been run against a live project, and that is written down rather than assumed.

stages.title: People and access
stages.why: The unlock. Four separate blockers clear here, and nothing below can be tested by the people who will actually use it until they can log in.

ships: Staff records tied to auth users, scoped to tenant and property
Invite by email, accept, deactivate
Names replace raw uuids everywhere approver and receiver are shown
shipments.proof: Invite a staff member, they accept and appear; a discount they approve shows their name, not a uuid

shipments.t: Role permission matrix and the front-desk login fix
ships: Replace the blunt requireAdmin gate with per-permission checks
Permission matrix: front desk, housekeeping, storekeeper, kitchen, bar, manager, owner
Server-side enforcement in the RPCs, not just hidden nav
shipments.proof: A front-desk account logs in, sees only its nav, and a blocked RPC called directly is refused by the database, not by the screen
shipments.note: Gate today: requireAdmin at App.tsx:72, failing closed at ProtectedRoute.tsx:70 against ADMIN_ROLES = owner, manager in types/auth.ts:23.

ships: Which actions demand a manager PIN becomes configuration, not code
Threshold rules per action
shipments.proof: Turn the PIN requirement on for an action and watch it refuse without one

ships: Staff assigned to locations
Location selector shows only what the user may see
Requisition badge wired to real permissions
Quantity and money are separate permissions: a storekeeper sees quantities and reorder levels because that is their daily job, while cost, value and margin are the manager's and owner's view
shipments.proof: A barman login sees Bar only. A storekeeper sees Store. Neither can post to the other, checked server-side.
shipments.note: Revised 16 Aug after Lanre's challenge: do NOT hide stock quantities from the storekeeper — knowing what is low and when to buy IS the job. The split that matters is quantity versus money, not visible versus hidden. Blindness on a stock take is a property of the COUNT SHEET plus who does the counting; in a small hotel the count is usually done by someone other than the custodian, which is the real control and is organisational rather than software. Where one person does both, the sheet is still blind, the variance is still attributed, and the manager reviewing the variance is the control.

shipments.t: Activity log the manager can read
ships: Readable view over change_log
Filter by person, date, action
shipments.proof: A discount, a reversal and a stock adjustment all appear with names and reasons

ships: A tax rate carries the date it takes effect, so a change announced in October and effective 1 January is TYPED IN in October
The rate a charge is taxed at is resolved from the charge's own business date, not from whatever is live when it is posted
The existing captured rows are what history reads; this changes only which rate a NEW charge captures
shipments.proof: A rate effective 1 January is entered in October; a charge posted on 31 December captures the old rate and one posted on 1 January captures the new one, with nobody touching anything at midnight. A charge posted in February but DATED 31 December captures the December rate.
shipments.note: WHAT 058 DELIBERATELY DOES NOT COVER, scheduled rather than left to be rediscovered as a surprise. 058 captures what a charge was taxed at the moment it is posted, which makes every bill ever issued immune to a later rate change and is the whole of the problem it set out to solve. Two things remain, and they are the two cases where capture still captures the wrong number or captures it late. FIRST, A SCHEDULED CHANGE. A rate announced in October and effective 1 January has to be typed in by a human at midnight. A hotel without a controller charges the old rate for a week, and the system cannot currently prevent it — there is nowhere to put the future rate. SECOND, AND THIS IS THE SHARPER ONE, A BACK-DATED CHARGE. post_charge takes p_charge_date verbatim: there is no past-date guard, measured in the function rather than assumed. So a charge posted today with a business date before a rate change takes TODAY's rate rather than the rate that applied on its own date, and 058 then makes that figure permanent instead of making it correct. Capture is the right foundation and is not the whole answer. The in-place UPDATE of a rate stays, deliberately: once charges carry their own rate the audit answer comes from the charge rather than from the rate table, and a second mechanism would have to do something capture does not. Effective dating is that something, which is why it is a shipment and not a footnote.

Board view of the whole property

Counts that match the database

Petty cash float and expenses paid at the property

AND THE PAYOUT A REFUND IS NOT. 067's ceiling refuses a refund larger than what the folio received and its hint sends the user here by name, so this shipment owes that case a real destination: money leaving the building against no receipt, with its own approval and its own account. Until it ships, the refusal is correct and the alternative is a manual journal — which is the honest state of it, not a gap nobody noticed

stages.title: The owner's view, then go live
stages.why: Small to build, and it is what makes the owner trust the system enough to stop running the spreadsheet in parallel.

ships: REVENUE BY ACCOUNT, and with it MISC'S EXPIRY CONDITION (068's ruling, 044's model). Miscellaneous is a deliberate named bucket and not a fallback — but a bucket nobody ever empties stops being honest. When this report exists: if Other revenue carries a material share of a month's revenue, the charges inside it have earned their own categories, and the report is where somebody sees that rather than a note nobody revisits. A deferral with no trigger is a thing nobody ever comes back to
Occupancy, ADR, RevPAR, revenue by category

WHEN THE FEE IS ADDED, reverse_cancel HAS TO TAKE IT BACK OFF. Today a cancellation posts nothing, so reversing one has nothing to unwind and the books agree. shipments.note: THE KNOWN-COST LIST. Each of these was noticed while building something else, left deliberately because it is right at this size, and written down so the performance pass measures rather than hunts. None is a defect today and none should be optimised before it is measured — the point of recording them is that the next person does not rediscover them one at a time. (1) 051, the unvaluable movement count: it comes from the same subquery as the value so there is one definition of what unvaluable means, which is correct and costs a pass over the position's movements per row of the reconciliation. (2) 051's correlated subquery, for the same reason and in the same place. (3) 056, purchase_order_settled_status(): the transition trigger calls it on EVERY status update, and it scans the order's receipt lines. That is what makes the status unable to be a lie — the trigger checks the claim rather than the caller — so the cost is bought deliberately and the alternatives were worse. One order's receipt lines is a handful of rows at Heledon; it is worth knowing at a year of trading, and worth knowing again if a tenant ever has orders with hundreds of deliveries against them. The answer, when it is measured, is NOT a counter column: that is rule 6's cache with no recompute function, and 036 already says what to do instead if it ever stops being cheap.
